claim: The primate amygdala performs multiple functions that may be related to the anatomical heterogeneity of its nuclei.
source: The primate amygdala performs multiple functions that may be related to the anatomical heterogeneity of its nuclei.
evidence: This is a general statement about amygdala function and structure that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: Individual neurons with stimulus- and task-specific responses are not clustered in any of the nuclei.
source: Individual neurons with stimulus- and task-specific responses are not clustered in any of the nuclei, suggesting that single-units may be too-fine grained to shed light on the mesoscale organization of the amygdala.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the authors' observations and previous work.

claim: Local field potentials recorded simultaneously from multiple locations within the primate amygdala contain spatially defined and statistically separable responses to visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli.
source: We have extracted from local field potentials recorded simultaneously from multiple locations within the primate (Macaca mulatta) amygdala spatially defined and statistically separable responses to visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A generalized eigendecomposition-based method of source separation isolated coactivity patterns that correspond to putative subnetworks.
source: A generalized eigendecomposition-based method of source separation isolated coactivity patterns, or components, that in neurophysiological terms correspond to putative subnetworks.
evidence: This describes the analytical method and its interpretation, supported by the data analysis performed.

claim: Some component spatial patterns mapped onto the anatomical organization of the amygdala, while other components reflected integration across nuclei.
source: Some component spatial patterns mapped onto the anatomical organization of the amygdala, while other components reflected integration across nuclei.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the component mapping analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The components differentiated between visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli suggesting the presence of functionally distinct parallel subnetworks.
source: These components differentiated between visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli suggesting the presence of functionally distinct parallel subnetworks.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by time-frequency analysis data.

claim: The division of the amygdala into nuclei reflects the developmental origins and the input-output connections of each nucleus with other structures.
source: The division of the amygdala into nuclei reflects the developmental origins and the input-output connections of each nucleus with other structures (Amaral et al., 1992; Pessoa et al., 2019; Swanson and Petrovich, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cell-type-specific circuit dissection of the rodent amygdala revealed further compartmentalization of the amygdala.
source: Cell-type-specific circuit dissection of the rodent amygdala revealed further compartmentalization of the amygdala (reviewed by Duvarci and Pare, 2014; Fadok et al., 2018; Gafford and Ressler, 2016; Janak and Tye, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The anatomical compartmentalization is rarely reproduced by the response properties of single neurons.
source: However, the anatomical compartmentalization is rarely reproduced by the response properties of single neurons (e.g., Beyeler et al., 2018; Kyriazi et al., 2018; Morrow et al., 2019; Putnam and Gothard, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies including the authors' own work.

claim: Local field potentials reflect the aggregate activity of hundreds to tens of thousands of neurons.
source: The local field potentials (LFPs), reflecting the aggregate activity of hundreds to tens of thousands of neurons (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Einevoll et al., 2013; Pesaran et al., 2018), may provide a more adequate mesoscopic-scale view of intra-amygdala activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on LFP properties.

claim: Task-relevant LFP signals have been successfully extracted from the amygdala of non-primate species in the context of fear conditioning, anticipatory anxiety, and reward learning.
source: Although task-relevant LFP signals have been successfully extracted from the amygdala of non-primate species in the context of fear conditioning (Courtin et al., 2014; Paré et al., 2002; Seidenbecher et al., 2003; Stujenske et al., 2014), anticipatory anxiety (Paré et al., 2002), and reward learning (Popescu et al., 2009), remarkably little is known about the information content of the local field potentials in the primate amygdala.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in non-primate species.

claim: Remarkably little is known about the information content of the local field potentials in the primate amygdala.
source: Although task-relevant LFP signals have been successfully extracted from the amygdala of non-primate species in the context of fear conditioning (Courtin et al., 2014; Paré et al., 2002; Seidenbecher et al., 2003; Stujenske et al., 2014), anticipatory anxiety (Paré et al., 2002), and reward learning (Popescu et al., 2009), remarkably little is known about the information content of the local field potentials in the primate amygdala.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on literature review.

claim: The majority of multisensory neurons in the monkey amygdala respond to visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli and discriminate between sensory modalities via different spike train metrics.
source: We recently reported that the majority of multisensory neurons in the monkey amygdala not only respond to visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli, but also discriminate, via different spike train metrics, between sensory modalities and even between individual stimuli of the same sensory modality (Morrow et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Multisensory neurons and neurons selective for a particular sensory modality were not clustered in any nucleus or subnuclear region.
source: Multisensory neurons and neurons selective for a particular sensory modality were not clustered in any nucleus or subnuclear region, suggesting an organization scheme in spatially distributed but functionally coordinated networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' previous findings.

claim: The combined excitatory, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory effects elicited by different sensory modalities would be better captured in the dynamics of the LFPs than by the response properties of single neurons.
source: We expected that the combined excitatory, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory effects elicited by different sensory modalities would be better captured in the dynamics of the LFPs than by the response properties of single neurons (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Mazzoni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Stimuli of different sensory modalities elicit different spatiotemporal patterns of activity in the local field potentials recorded from linear arrays of electrodes.
source: Specifically, we explored the hypothesis that stimuli of different sensory modalities elicit different spatiotemporal patterns of activity in the local field potentials recorded from linear arrays of electrodes.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis tested in the study, supported by the experimental data.

claim: GED has been shown to reliably reconstruct network-level LFP dynamics in both simulated and empirical data that are often missed by conventional methods of source-separation.
source: GED has been shown to reliably reconstruct network-level LFP dynamics in both simulated and empirical data that are often missed by conventional methods of source-separation (Cohen, 2017a; de Cheveigné and Parra, 2014; Parra et al., 2005; Van Veen et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: Multiple, statistically dissociable patterns of subnetwork activity tied to the functional and spatial structure of the amygdala were discovered that were missed by the analysis of single-unit activity.
source: Here, we adapted this method to our data and discovered multiple, statistically dissociable patterns of subnetwork activity tied to the functional and spatial structure of the amygdala that was missed by the analysis of single-unit activity (Morrow et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the data analysis.

claim: LFPs were monitored simultaneously from the entire dorso-ventral expanse of the amygdala using linear electrode arrays with 16 equidistant contacts at 400 μm spacing.
source: We monitored LFPs simultaneously from the entire dorso-ventral expanse of the amygdala using linear electrode arrays (V-probes, Plexon Inc, Dallas, TX) that have 16 equidistant contacts (400 μm spacing, Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Signals were referenced to the common average across the 16 contacts to ensure that signals were locally generated and not volume conducted from distant regions.
source: In each session the signals were referenced to the common average across the 16 contacts; this ensured that our signals were locally generated and not volume conducted from distant regions.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice and its rationale.

claim: All trials were separated by a 3–4 s inter-trial interval and preceded by a visual fixation cue.
source: All trials were separated by a 3–4 s inter-trial interval (ITI) and preceded by a visual fixation cue presented at the center of a monitor in front of the animal.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: All trials were followed by a brief delay (0.7–1.4 s) before a small consistent amount of juice was delivered.
source: All trials were followed by a brief delay (0.7–1.4 s) before a small consistent amount of juice was delivered.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: 95% of the contacts showed significant changes in LFP activity relative to baseline.
source: Ninety-five percent of the contacts showed significant changes in LFP activity relative to baseline (623/656, 95.0% of all contacts, Wilcoxon rank-sum tests; Bonferroni corrected for 16 comparisons, ɑ = 0.01/16 = 0.000625).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Between 1 and 5 simultaneously active and statistically significant components were found during each recording session.
source: We found between 1 and 5 simultaneously active and statistically significant components during each recording session (Figure 2h–i), leading to a total of 116 components obtained from 41 sessions (significance was computed via permutation testing with corrections for multiple comparisons; see Methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the GED analysis.

claim: A total of 116 components were obtained from 41 sessions.
source: We found between 1 and 5 simultaneously active and statistically significant components during each recording session (Figure 2h–i), leading to a total of 116 components obtained from 41 sessions (significance was computed via permutation testing with corrections for multiple comparisons; see Methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the data.

claim: Removing non-amygdala contacts from the analysis eliminated 24 components, leaving 92 components attributable solely to activity recorded in the amygdala.
source: Removing these contacts from the analysis eliminated 24 components (i.e., 92 components were attributable solely to activity recorded in the amygdala), emphasizing the importance of the spatial location of each contact (Figure 2j–k).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the spatial analysis.

claim: The boundaries of the statistical clusters matched both internal and external anatomical boundaries of the amygdala.
source: The boundaries of the statistical clusters matched both internal and external anatomical boundaries of the amygdala (Figure 3), which were estimated through a combination of high-resolution MRI and histology (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the component mapping analysis and anatomical verification.

claim: GED is a purely statistical decomposition that is not constrained by anatomical information, spatial arrangement, or relative distances of the electrode positions.
source: This is important because GED is a purely statistical decomposition that is not constrained by anatomical information, spatial arrangement, or relative distances of the electrode positions.
evidence: This describes a property of the GED method.

claim: The GED method discovered subnuclear divisions that neuroimaging would not be able to detect but are well known from histological analyses.
source: Moreover, this method discovered subnuclear divisions that neuroimaging would not be able to detect but are well known from histological analyses.
evidence: This is an inference about the capabilities of the method compared to other techniques.

claim: The horizontal dotted lines intersecting the basal nucleus in Figure 3e and f correspond to known boundaries between the magnocellular, intermediate, and parvocellular subdivisions.
source: For example, in Figure 3e and f the horizontal dotted lines intersecting the basal nucleus correspond to known boundaries between the magnocellular, intermediate, and parvocellular subdivisions (Amaral et al., 1992).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the figure data supported by citation to anatomical literature.

claim: The overall number of matching contacts between statistical grouping and anatomical grouping was 723/1072 (67.4%).
source: The overall number of matching contacts was 723/1072 (67.4%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the anatomical-statistical comparison.

claim: Only the first components showed statistically better than chance overlap between statistical grouping and anatomical grouping of contacts.
source: Only the first components showed statistically better than chance overlap (249/349, 71.3%, paired t-test, t = 2.76, df = 40, p=0.009, 1000 permutations, Bonferroni corrected for five comparisons, ɑ = 0.05/5 = 0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: Each subnetwork responded selectively to visual, tactile, or auditory stimuli or a combination thereof.
source: Time-frequency analyses of the component time series showed that each subnetwork responded selectively to visual, tactile, or auditory stimuli or a combination thereof (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the time-frequency analysis.

claim: Of the 116 identified components, 102 discriminated between sensory modalities in at least one frequency range for at least one sensory modality.
source: Of the 116 identified components, 102 discriminated between sensory modalities in at least one frequency range for at least one sensory modality (cluster-mass t-tests, ɑ = 0.01, see Methods), as shown by the change in power elicited by stimuli of each sensory modality (Figure 4a–f).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: Only 13 out of 102 components showed responses restricted to a single sensory modality.
source: Only 13 out of these 102 components showed responses restricted to a single sensory modality.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis.

claim: The majority of sensory signals processed in the amygdala are multisensory.
source: These results replicate, at a larger spatial scale, our findings from the single unit analyses (Morrow et al., 2019), that is, that the majority of sensory signals processed in the amygdala are multisensory.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and comparison to previous work.

claim: Sensory modalities were better differentiated at lower frequencies.
source: Sensory modalities were better differentiated at lower frequencies (Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, ɑ = 0.01; Figure 4g).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the frequency data.

claim: Visual stimuli elicited larger power changes than tactile, which in turn elicited larger changes than auditory stimuli in components with multisensory responses.
source: The same observation holds when only assessing components with multisensory responses (72/89 components) (Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, ɑ = 0.01; Figure 4h–j); visual stimuli elicited larger power changes than tactile, which in turn elicited larger changes than auditory stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of multisensory components.

claim: The spectral profile from the first component roughly followed the 1/f function typically observed in LFP signals.
source: While the spectral profile from the first component roughly followed the 1/f function typically observed in LFP signals, the subsequent spectra showed peaks around the delta (3.5–4.5 Hz), theta (6-8), low-gamma (~38 Hz), and high-gamma (63–75 Hz) frequency bands.
evidence: This is an observation from the spectral analysis compared to known LFP properties.

claim: The subsequent spectra showed peaks around the delta (3.5–4.5 Hz), theta (6-8), low-gamma (~38 Hz), and high-gamma (63–75 Hz) frequency bands.
source: While the spectral profile from the first component roughly followed the 1/f function typically observed in LFP signals, the subsequent spectra showed peaks around the delta (3.5–4.5 Hz), theta (6-8), low-gamma (~38 Hz), and high-gamma (63–75 Hz) frequency bands.
evidence: This is a finding from the spectral analysis.

claim: The prominent spectral peaks at 4, 7, 38, and 70 Hz were preserved after removing non-amygdala contacts.
source: While some changes in the spectra were expected from the removal of non-amygdala contacts, it is noteworthy that the prominent spectral peaks (for example, at 4, 7, 38, and 70 Hz) were preserved (Figure 4l).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of spectral profiles with and without non-amygdala contacts.

claim: The primate amygdala exhibits prominent rhythms at peaks often observed in the cortex.
source: The preservation of these spectral peaks after removing possible influence of non-amygdala electrodes shows that the primate amygdala exhibits prominent rhythms at peaks often observed in the cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spectral analysis and comparison to cortical rhythms.

claim: No significant differences were observed between the number of components extracted via modality-specific GED for visual (81), tactile (79), and auditory (71) stimuli.
source: No significant differences were observed between the number of components (visual = 81, tactile = 79, and auditory = 71) extracted via modality-specific GED (χ2 = 0.37, p=0.83) (Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the modality-specific analysis.

claim: The sensory-modality-specific component maps were significantly correlated with the component maps that combined all three sensory modalities.
source: Furthermore, the sensory-modality-specific component maps were significantly correlated with the component maps that combined all three sensory modalities (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis.

claim: The component maps based solely on visual trials matched better the nuclear boundaries than the component maps based only on either auditory or tactile trials.
source: We found, however, that the component maps based solely on visual trials matched better the nuclear boundaries than the component maps based only on either auditory or tactile trials (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the anatomical comparison analysis.

claim: The changepoint positions in the first and second visual component maps coincided with the estimated anatomical boundaries of the nuclei.
source: Specifically, the changepoint positions in the first and second visual component maps coincided with the estimated anatomical boundaries of the nuclei (paired t-tests, p=0.0006 and p=0.001, respectively; same parameters as previous analyses, see Table 1 for full stats).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the anatomical comparison.

claim: The main GED findings reflect a mixture of sensory-independent and sensory-dependent functional organization.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the main GED findings reflect a mixture of sensory-independent and sensory-dependent functional organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modality-specific analysis.

claim: Only a few single unit studies reported an uneven distribution of neurons with particular response properties across the nuclei.
source: Only a few single unit studies reported an uneven distribution of neurons with particular response properties across the nuclei (e.g., Grabenhorst et al., 2019, Grabenhorst et al., 2016; Mosher et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of previous literature supported by citations.

claim: An increasing number of single unit studies reported that neurons in the amygdala respond to multiple stimulus dimensions and task parameters.
source: To complicate things further, an increasing number of single unit studies reported that neurons in the amygdala respond to multiple stimulus dimensions and task parameters (Kyriazi et al., 2018; Morrow et al., 2019; Munuera et al., 2018; Putnam and Gothard, 2019; Saez et al., 2015; Gothard, 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of recent literature supported by citations.

claim: Multidimensional neurons are not clustered in any nuclei or subnuclear region, which seems to be at odds with the compartmentalized view of the amygdala.
source: These multidimensional neurons are not clustered in any nuclei or subnuclear region, which seems to be at odds with the compartmentalized view of the amygdala.
evidence: This is an observation from the literature and an inference about its implications.

claim: Remarkably little is known about the neurophysiology of the primate amygdala at the network level.
source: Remarkably little is known about the neurophysiology of the primate amygdala at the network level, due in part to its layerless architecture that is not expected to generate the predictable LFP patterns observed in layered structures like the neocortex or the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field.

claim: The layerless architecture of the amygdala is not expected to generate the predictable LFP patterns observed in layered structures like the neocortex or the hippocampus.
source: Remarkably little is known about the neurophysiology of the primate amygdala at the network level, due in part to its layerless architecture that is not expected to generate the predictable LFP patterns observed in layered structures like the neocortex or the hippocampus.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about LFP generation in different brain structures.

claim: Each nucleus and nuclear subregion of the primate amygdala has different cytoarchitecture and distinct input-output connections with both cortical and subcortical structures.
source: In the primate amygdala, each nucleus and nuclear subregion has different cytoarchitecture and also distinct input-output connections with both cortical and subcortical structures (Amaral et al., 1992; Ghashghaei and Barbas, 2002; Sah et al., 2003, Pessoa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Projections from the amygdala to dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra mainly arise from the central nucleus.
source: For example, projections from the amygdala to dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra mainly arise from the central nucleus.
evidence: This is an example of anatomical connectivity.

claim: Central nucleus projections are further distinguished into medial and lateral subdivisions that terminate in separate subregions of the substantia nigra.
source: These central nucleus projections are further distinguished into medial and lateral subdivisions that terminate in separate subregions of the substantia nigra (Fudge and Haber, 2000).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The subregions of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex are reciprocally connected to distinct nuclear subdivisions of the basolateral complex.
source: Likewise, the subregions of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex are reciprocally connected to distinct nuclear subdivisions of the basolateral complex (Amaral and Price, 1984; Ghashghaei and Barbas, 2002).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: This anatomical organization could give rise to parallel, nucleus-anchored processing loops that induce nuclear-specific patterns of neural activity.
source: This organization could give rise to parallel, nucleus-anchored processing loops that induce nuclear-specific patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The rich intra-amygdala connectivity could distribute signals arriving to or originating from a particular area of the amygdala across multiple nuclei, evening out functional differences expected based on structural consideration alone.
source: It is also possible that the rich intra-amygdala connectivity (Bonda, 2000; Pitkänen and Amaral, 1991) distributes signals arriving to or originating from a particular area of the amygdala across multiple nuclei, evening out functional differences expected based on structural consideration alone.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: The human neuroimaging literature alluded to mesoscopic organization based on anatomical connectivity or resting state fMRI data.
source: The human neuroimaging literature already alluded to this type of organization, based on anatomical connectivity (Bickart et al., 2012) or resting state fMRI data (Roy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a summary of previous neuroimaging literature supported by citations.

claim: Evidence is provided for a mesoscopic organization of the amygdala into putative subnetworks that often respect nuclear boundaries but in some cases reflect synchronization of neural populations across multiple subnuclear regions.
source: Here, we provide evidence for a mesoscopic organization of the amygdala, into putative subnetworks that often respect nuclear boundaries, but in some cases reflect synchronization of neural populations across multiple subnuclear regions, that were identified by guided source separation of the local field potentials recorded from multi-contact electrodes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The presence of any identifiable subnetworks demonstrates that a layered architecture is not a prerequisite for meaningful organization of LFP activity.
source: The presence of any identifiable subnetworks demonstrates that a layered architecture is not a prerequisite for meaningful organization of LFP activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: The presence of multiple subnetworks suggests functional compartmentalization.
source: The presence of multiple subnetworks suggests functional compartmentalization.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: The strongest of the subnetworks were contoured by the internal and external boundaries of the nuclei of the amygdala.
source: Importantly, the strongest of the subnetworks were contoured by the internal and external boundaries of the nuclei of the amygdala.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the component mapping analysis.

claim: A mesoscale physiological feature of the amygdala (the LFP), unlike the single units, is bound by anatomical constraints.
source: This is evidence that a mesoscale physiological feature of the amygdala (the LFP), unlike the single units, is bound by anatomical constraints.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing LFP and single-unit findings.

claim: Expanding GED to three-dimensions using multiple linear electrode arrays at different medio-lateral and rostral-caudal positions will likely generate a more complete functional map of the primate amygdala.
source: The implications of this finding are twofold: (1) expanding GED to three-dimensions (using multiple linear electrode arrays at different medio-lateral and rostral-caudal positions) will likely generate a more complete functional map of the primate amygdala, and (2) these new physiological features revealed by GED can then be set in register with the known neuroanatomy encompassing all nuclei.
evidence: This is a speculation about future experiments.

claim: The use of a single electrode array limited the assessment of network structure along a single axis (dorsal-ventral) that was dependent on the angle of insertion of the probe.
source: For example, the use of a single electrode array limited us to assessing network structure along a single axis (i.e., dorsal-ventral) that was dependent on the angle of insertion of the probe.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the current study.

claim: By collecting LFP from contacts on additional arrays placed at different medial-lateral and anterior-posterior positions, component maps could be constructed in multiple planes that intersect the nuclei of the amygdala.
source: By collecting LFP from contacts on additional arrays placed at different medial-lateral and anterior-posterior positions, component maps could be constructed in multiple planes that intersect the nuclei of the amygdala.
evidence: This is a proposal for future experiments.

claim: Multi-array recordings would better localize the sources of the LFP signals and provide a platform for testing anatomy-based hypotheses regarding non-contiguous inter-nuclear subnetworks.
source: These experiments will better localize the sources of the LFP signals and provide a platform for testing anatomy-based hypotheses regarding non-contiguous (i.e., spatially distributed) inter-nuclear subnetworks (Pitkänen et al., 1995; Pitkänen and Amaral, 1991; Sah et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculation about the benefits of future experiments.

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated inter-nuclear differences in decoding accuracy obtained from pseudo-populations of neurons for various task-related parameters using nearest-neighbor and support-vector machine classifiers.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated inter-nuclear differences in decoding accuracy obtained from pseudo-populations of neurons for various task-related parameters using nearest-neighbor and support-vector machine classifiers (Grabenhorst et al., 2019; Grabenhorst et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of recent literature supported by citations.

claim: GED analyses could be used to generate components that maximally differentiate signals based on task parameters.
source: In future experiments, GED analyses could be used to generate components that maximally differentiate signals based on similar task parameters.
evidence: This is a proposal for future experiments.

claim: Comparisons of component mapping to the results obtained from decoding methodologies would provide complimentary metrics for examining the structure-function relationships of single unit and LFP activity.
source: Comparisons of component mapping to the results obtained from these decoding methodologies would provide complimentary metrics for examining the structure-function relationships of single unit and LFP activity.
evidence: This is a speculation about future analyses.

claim: The subnetworks identified by GED are functionally relevant because the coactivity patterns elicited by visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli discriminated between sensory modalities.
source: The subnetworks identified by GED are functionally relevant because the coactivity patterns elicited by visual, tactile, and auditory stimuli discriminated between sensory modalities (as shown in Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-frequency analysis.

claim: No activity pattern was specific for a particular sensory modality, but the majority of activity patterns carried information about one or multiple sensory modalities.
source: While no activity pattern was specific for a particular sensory modality, the majority of activity patterns carried information about one or multiple sensory modalities.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the time-frequency analysis.

claim: The activity of the subnetwork shown in Figure 4e conveys information about all sensory modalities albeit with different power in each frequency band, without any one frequency band being assigned to a single sensory modality.
source: For example, the activity of the subnetwork shown in Figure 4e conveys information about all sensory modalities albeit with different power in each frequency band, without any one frequency band being assigned to a single sensory modality.
evidence: This is an interpretation of a specific example from the data.

claim: Modality-specific analyses further support the hypothesis that functional subnetworks in the amygdala process multisensory information.
source: Modality-specific analyses further support the hypothesis that functional subnetworks in the amygdala process multisensory information (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modality-specific analysis.

claim: These results complement the selectivity and specificity pattern of the single-unit responses recorded simultaneously from the same contacts.
source: These results complement the selectivity and specificity pattern of the single-unit responses recorded simultaneously from the same contacts (Morrow et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings from the same dataset.

claim: Visual stimuli elicited larger increases in low-frequency (<10 Hz) power compared to tactile and auditory stimuli.
source: There were, however, two notable areas where the components were sensitive to sensory modality: (1) Visual stimuli elicited larger increases in low-frequency (<10 Hz) power (Figure 4g–i); and (2) only the visual components significantly mapped onto MRI-defined nuclear boundaries.
evidence: This is a finding from the frequency analysis.

claim: Only the visual components significantly mapped onto MRI-defined nuclear boundaries.
source: There were, however, two notable areas where the components were sensitive to sensory modality: (1) Visual stimuli elicited larger increases in low-frequency (<10 Hz) power (Figure 4g–i); and (2) only the visual components significantly mapped onto MRI-defined nuclear boundaries.
evidence: This is a finding from the anatomical mapping analysis.

claim: The visual bias in component mapping is consistent with anatomical tract tracing studies that found a preponderance of projections to the amygdala from visual areas.
source: This is consistent with the outcome of anatomical tract tracing studies that compared inputs to the primate amygdala from visual, auditory, tactile, and multisensory areas of the temporal lobe and found a preponderance of projections to the amygdala from visual areas (Amaral and Price, 1984; Amaral et al., 1992; Stefanacci and Amaral, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in light of anatomical literature.

claim: The mesoscopic intranuclear spatial structure of the multisensory subnetworks is driven predominantly by visual processing.
source: Thus, the mesoscopic intranuclear spatial structure of the multisensory subnetworks is driven predominantly by visual processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the visual dominance in the data.

claim: The single-unit data collected in these experiments did not show a bias towards the visual modality.
source: Interestingly, the single-unit data collected in these experiments (Morrow et al., 2019) did not show this bias towards the visual modality.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings from the same dataset.

claim: The LFP contains information that was not readily accessible from the spiking data alone.
source: This shows that the LFP contains information that was not readily accessible from the spiking data alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing LFP and single-unit findings.

claim: Stimulus-related motor responses could account, at least in part, for the observed pattern of activity.
source: Without monitoring eye movements or facial movements, we can neither confirm nor deny alternative explanations, such as stimulus-related motor responses that could account, at least in part, for the observed pattern of activity.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of an alternative explanation that cannot be ruled out.

claim: Neurons in the amygdala respond with phasic bursts of activity to fixations on certain components of images such as faces and eyes.
source: Indeed, neurons in the amygdala respond with phasic bursts of activity to fixations on certain components of images such as faces (Minxha et al., 2017) and eyes (Mosher et al., 2014), and during production of facial expressions (Livneh et al., 2012; Mosher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in the amygdala respond with phasic bursts of activity during production of facial expressions.
source: Indeed, neurons in the amygdala respond with phasic bursts of activity to fixations on certain components of images such as faces (Minxha et al., 2017) and eyes (Mosher et al., 2014), and during production of facial expressions (Livneh et al., 2012; Mosher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Further progress in understanding the mesoscale organization of the primate amygdala will come from expanding the network analyses to cover field-field or spike-field interactions between the amygdala and connected structures.
source: Further progress in understanding the mesoscale organization of the primate amygdala will come from expanding the network analyses presented here to cover field-field or spike-field interactions between the amygdala and connected structures.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: The first few attempts at analyzing interactions between the amygdala and the anterior cingulate cortex have been successful in revealing the directionality of interactions during aversive learning.
source: The first few attempts in this direction have been successful in revealing the directionality of interactions between the amygdala and the anterior cingulate cortex during aversive learning (Taub et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of previous work supported by citation.

claim: Brain-wide circuits are the domain where LFP analyses might be most revealing.
source: Brain-wide circuits are indeed the domain where LFP analyses might be most revealing (Pesaran et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an opinion supported by citation to previous work.
